Complex numbers are known through polar form and roots of unity, and binary and two's-complement representation through computer organization. Each subject is taken only to first-course depth: no abstract algebra beyond the fields and rings that linear algebra uses, no Fourier analysis beyond the finite transform, no number theory beyond gcd, primes and modular inverses, and nothing from coding theory, circuit complexity or the specialist finite-network material.

26	## Pages, in reading order
27	
28	- `polynomial-ring`: Polynomial ring modulo y^r + 1: The ring of polynomials with complex coefficients of degree less than r, where r is a power of two and y^r is identified with −1, so that multiplication by a power of y is a signed cyclic shift of the coefficient list.
29	- `polynomial-roots-of-unity`: Polynomial roots of unity: The observation that powers of y in the polynomial ring are roots of unity whose multiplication is a signed shift, so a transform over the ring can use them as twiddle factors.
30	- `two-point-butterfly`: Normalized two-point butterfly: The map (u, v) to ((u + v)/2, (u − v)/2) applied to a pair of coefficients, the basic step of the synthetic transforms.
31	- `gaussian-dyadic`: Gaussian dyadic: A complex number whose real and imaginary parts are dyadic rationals, that is, have power-of-two denominators.
32	- `linear-algebra`: Linear algebra over a field: Vector spaces, linear maps and matrices, with subspaces, bilinear forms, orthogonal complements and tensor products, as used by the finite networks and their labels.
33	- `fixed-tape-machine`: Fixed-tape Turing machine model: A machine with one fixed finite alphabet and one fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes, in which each step moves each head by at most one cell and running time counts these steps.
34	- `schonhage-strassen-conjecture`: Schönhage–Strassen optimality conjecture: The 1971 proposal that n log n is the optimal order of growth for multiplying integers on a multitape Turing machine; the main result refutes it in the fixed-tape model.
35	- `logical-volume`: Logical volume: The number V of stored data bits in an array, not counting work tapes or duplicate streams; every tape cost is measured against V.
36	- `address-fields`: Address fields and rows: An array is indexed by a complete lexicographic product of address fields and stored in that order, and a row is the complete block of entries at one fixed prefix and row index.
37	- `elementary-stream-operations`: Elementary stream operations: Linear-time scans on a fixed number of tapes that permute or move digits at chosen positions, apply fixed pointwise maps to aligned streams, and split whole rows cyclically into W streams of equal volume.
38	- `row-splitting`: Row splitting into role streams: Distributing the rows of an array cyclically among W role streams, so that each stream has the same shape and volume V/W and gates act pointwise on matching addresses.
39	- `controlled-shifts`: Controlled cyclic shifts: A cyclic shift of a target field by an offset computed from the preceding control fields, together with multiplication by fixed rational units, all done in linear time on tapes.
40	- `scratch-restoration`: Restoration of arbitrary scratch values: A linear computation whose auxiliary wires may start with arbitrary values and end with the same values, so that an exchange of two banks can be performed without knowing the scratch contents (the transparent-computation idea of Buhrman et al.).
41	- `triple-subset-exchange-network`: Triple-subset exchange network: A fixed linear network whose banks are indexed by triples of three-element subsets of a 100-element set, which exchanges two banks with a sign while restoring all scratch wires, using eight rows of copy, gather, scatter and side-injection operations.
42	- `frames`: Frames on network vertices: An invertible linear operator attached to each gate, source and sink of a network, which changes the stored representation of a wire's array so that every gate acts pointwise and the endpoint operators are the only net effect.
43	- `subspace-labels`: Subspace labels and orthogonal residuals: A nondegenerate subspace attached to each network vertex, with one label containing the other along every edge, so that the dimension of the orthogonal residual on an edge measures the cost of its frame change.
44	- `rank-saving`: Rank saving s < Wm: The inequality that the number s of smaller calls is less than W times m, where W is the number of wires and m the label dimension, which is the source of the power saving.
45	- `volume-normalized-recursion`: Volume-normalized recursion: A recursion in which cost per unit volume is multiplied by s/W at each level, with s/W below m to the power tau, so that the total cost is O(e^tau) per unit volume for chunks of e = m^k digits.
46	- `lower-triangular-factorization`: Lower-triangular factorization: Every rational matrix of rank a factors as an invertible lower-triangular matrix times a partial permutation matrix with exactly a ones, times another invertible lower-triangular matrix.
47	- `matrix-shear-interchange`: Matrix shear of address fields: The map (H, D) to (H + AD, D) on two groups of address fields for a fixed rational matrix A of rank a, performed with exactly a interchanges of field pairs and linear extra work.
48	- `circuit-to-address-permutation`: Finite circuit as address permutation: The transfer of a finite bit circuit with rational vertex matrices whose rank sum is below Wm into a permutation of address fields that applies the same shear to every wire role.
49	- `power-width-chunk-interchange`: Power-width chunk interchange: The interchange of two disjoint equal chunks of e = m^k digits in O(V e^tau) time, by splitting rows into W role streams, applying one shear per unit of rank on the streams, and recursing with the same fixed tapes.
50	- `arbitrary-width-chunk-interchange`: Arbitrary-width chunk interchange: The interchange of two equal bit chunks of arbitrary width u in O(V u^tau) time, by padding to a power of the radix, moving high digits into a row field, and handling the remaining width as a sum of power-width pieces in base m.
51	- `two-point-phase-kernel`: Two-point phase kernel: The 2 by 2 matrix C = aI + bX with a = (1 + i)/2 and b = (1 − i)/2, the Hadamard conjugate of the phase diag(1, i), which satisfies C² = X and C⁴ = I and is the one-bit kernel from which phase frames are built.
52	- `binary-phase-frames`: Binary phase frames: Frames indexed by binary subspace labels, built from the Hadamard transform and phases i raised to the Hamming weight of each label's projection, so that each edge change is a product of two-point phase kernels, one per residual basis vector.
53	- `packed-selected-bit-xor`: Packed selected-bit XOR: A linear-time operation that XORs the selected bits of one address chunk slot into the corresponding selected bits of another for all selected positions at once, using eight packed rotations of guarded segments followed by deterministic repair of the few addresses whose guards fail.
54	- `guard-bits`: Guard bits: Extra fractional and integer bits reserved in each coefficient so that every intermediate value of an exact butterfly layer is represented exactly, with a width bound that grows only as a fixed power of the number of selected axes.
55	- `disk-grid-arrays`: Disk-grid arrays: Arrays of coefficients lying in the complex unit disk and on the grid 2^(−p) times the Gaussian integers, which hold every approximate value in the algorithm.
56	- `grid-truncation`: Truncation to the precision grid: Rounding each real and imaginary part of a coefficient toward zero onto the grid of spacing 2^(−p), which keeps arrays in the disk and moves each entry by less than sqrt(2) times 2^(−p).
57	- `simultaneous-butterfly-layer`: Simultaneous butterfly layer: The application of the normalized two-point butterfly to the same selected bit position in each of D address chunks at once, computed exactly through binary phase frames and truncated once, at cost O(V d^(λ')) with λ' below one instead of D separate passes.
58	- `transform-layout`: Positional layout of transform axes: A positional permutation of record addresses that places the selected bits of all participating axes at a common offset in consecutive K-bit chunks, realized by single-bit moves and chunk interchanges so that the simultaneous layer applies.
59	- `cyclic-convolution`: Cyclic convolution: The convolution of two arrays indexed by a product of cyclic groups, in which each output entry sums products of input entries whose indices are added modulo the axis lengths.
60	- `radix-digit-convolution`: Radix-digit convolution: The reduction of multiplying two n-bit integers to a cyclic convolution of their radix-2^b digit sequences, each with q = ceil(n/b) digits, whose coefficients are at most q(2^b − 1)^2, which is below 2^(3b).
61	- `crt-coefficient-map`: Chinese-remainder coefficient map: The algebra isomorphism x ↦ product of x_i^(μ_i) from C[x]/(x^S − 1) to a tensor product of cyclic rings for pairwise coprime lengths s_i, which preserves cyclic convolution and turns the ordinary coefficient order into a mixed-radix order reached by controlled cyclic shifts.
62	- `negacyclic-twist`: Phase twist of the last coordinate: The isomorphism from the cyclic group algebra of length r to the polynomial ring that sends x to ζy with ζ = e^(πi/r), implemented by multiplying coefficient k by ζ^k and undone by multiplying by ζ^(−k).
63	- `discrete-fourier-transform`: Normalized discrete Fourier transform: The map (F_q u)_k = (1/q) times the sum over j of u_j e^(−2πi jk/q) on vectors of length q, together with its opposite-sign partner F_q^+, which turns cyclic convolution into pointwise products up to a known factor.
64	- `synthetic-transform`: Synthetic polynomial transform: A normalized radix-two transform over the polynomial ring whose twiddle factors are powers of y, so each round is a parallel butterfly followed by a signed shift and the whole transform is a contraction.

67	- `frequency-order-retention`: Retained frequency order: The stored record order produced by the forward synthetic transforms, which is preserved through a pointwise product so that the opposite transform consumes it without extra data movement.
68	- `hvdh-multiplier`: Established fixed-tape integer multiplier: Harvey and van der Hoeven's deterministic fixed-tape multiplication of N-bit integers in O(N log N) time, which the new algorithm calls as an ordinary subroutine on shorter records.
69	- `signed-coefficient-packing`: Signed coefficient packing: Evaluating two integer polynomials at a large base 2^(4p) so that one exact integer product yields all coefficient products, with signed carries recovered by centered residues; it is a signed form of Kronecker substitution.
70	- `ring-product`: Normalized polynomial-ring product: The normalized product f g / r of two disk-grid polynomials in the polynomial ring, computed exactly by signed packing into four integer products and returned truncated to the grid.
71	- `normalized-ring-convolution`: Normalized ring convolution: The bilinear contraction M_r(f, g) = (f ∗ g)/(rM) = (f ∗ g)/T on arrays over the polynomial ring, computed as two forward synthetic transforms, a pointwise ring product and an opposite transform.

73	- `contraction`: Contraction: A linear map that does not increase the maximum-modulus norm, so that an error in its input is not amplified when it is applied to an approximation.
74	- `gaussian-resampling`: Gaussian resampling: The identity P_s F_s = 2^(2α²) B_0 P_t F_t A, with contractions A and B_0 built from Gaussian weights, which expresses a length-s Fourier transform through a length-t transform when t/s is close to one, keeping the coordinate permutations inside the identity.

tools.name: Read

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.

- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

31	for every input length and disproves the $n\log n$ optimality conjecture
32	of Sch\"onhage and Strassen in this model.
33	\end{abstract}

36	\section{Introduction}
37	
38	Sch\"onhage and Strassen proved in 1971 that two $n$-bit integers can
39	be multiplied in $O(n\log n\log\log n)$ time on a multitape Turing
40	machine, and proposed $n\log n$ as the optimal order of growth
41	\cite[Section~1]{SchonhageStrassen1971}. After a sequence of improvements,
42	Harvey and van der Hoeven reached the unconditional $O(n\log n)$ upper
43	bound~\cite{HarveyHoeven2021}. We obtain a strict power saving in the
44	logarithmic factor, in the same fixed finite-tape model. The algorithm
45	uses linear combinations of intermediate data to reduce the cost of
46	both address rearrangement and Fourier-transform layers.
47	
48	For a binary string $x$ of length $n$, let $\operatorname{val}(x)$ be
49	its nonnegative integer value, with the leftmost bit most significant.
50	For $0\le z<2^k$, let $\operatorname{bin}_k(z)$ denote its binary
51	representation padded on the left to length $k$. We consider exact
52	multiplication: on input $x\#y$, with $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$, the output
53	must be $\operatorname{bin}_{2n}(\operatorname{val}(x)\operatorname{val}(y))$.
54	Write $\lg n=\max\{\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,1\}$.
55	
56	\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
57	There is one deterministic Turing machine $A$, with a fixed finite
58	alphabet and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes, that
59	computes this exact product for every $n\ge1$ and every pair of $n$-bit
60	inputs. Its worst-case running time satisfies
61	\[
62	 T_A(n)=O\!\left(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa}\right),
63	 \qquad \kappa=2^{-182}.
64	\]
65	\end{theorem}
66	
67	The bound is asymptotic through all input lengths. The constants and
68	thresholds in the construction are extremely large; the algorithm is
69	intended to establish a bit-complexity bound. The theorem refutes an
70	eventual $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound for every fixed multiplication
71	machine in this model.
72	
73	\subsection{The two tape operations}
74	
75	Splitting the inputs into radix digits reduces multiplication to
76	convolution of short integer coefficients. Our starting point is the
77	Gaussian-resampling reduction of Harvey and van der Hoeven
78	\cite{HarveyHoeven2021}: it replaces the Fourier transforms needed for
79	this convolution by multidimensional transforms whose axis lengths are
80	powers of two. After a further conversion to convolution, one coordinate
81	is stored as the coefficient list of a polynomial modulo $y^r+1$, with $r$ a power of two. Powers of $y$ then
82	serve as roots of unity in the remaining axes, and multiplication by
83	such a root is a signed shift of the coefficient list. These are the
84	synthetic polynomial transforms of Nussbaumer and Quandalle and
85	Nussbaumer~\cite{NussbaumerQuandalle1978,Nussbaumer1980}.
86	
87	In this representation, the transform calculation consists of address
88	rearrangements, signed shifts, and two-point butterfly operations.
89	Scanning an array of $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of
90	$\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels already costs $\Theta(n\log n)$.
91	We therefore need savings in both movement and arithmetic. Two tape
92	procedures supply them; in both bounds, $V$ denotes the stored bit volume.
93	
94	The first procedure interchanges two disjoint contiguous address fields
95	of $u$ bits in an array whose addresses form a complete Cartesian
96	product. Its cost is $O(Vu^\tau)$ for a fixed $\tau<1$.
97	Although its final effect is an exact permutation, its intermediate
98	steps form pointwise XOR combinations of data. The final permutation is
99	exact for arbitrary initial auxiliary values.
100	
101	The second procedure applies
102	\[
103	 H_0(u,v)=\bigl((u+v)/2,(u-v)/2\bigr)
104	\]
105	simultaneously on selected coordinate bits of the numerical arrays.
106	Each record is a polynomial with complex fixed-point coefficients, and
107	$H_0$ acts coefficientwise. On the layouts used in the multiplication
108	algorithm, one selects the same bit position in each of at most $d$
109	equal-width address chunks, and the cost is $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ for a
110	fixed $\lambda'<1$. Intermediate values are exact Gaussian dyadics,
111	whose real and imaginary parts have power-of-two denominators. A single
112	truncation follows the completed contractive layer.
113	Section~\ref{sec:tape-interchange} proves the address bound, and
114	Section~\ref{sec:fast-butterfly-layers} gives the numerical layout,
115	precision hypotheses, and layer bound.
116	
117	\subsection{Linear networks and the recursive saving}
118	
119	Each procedure arises from its own fixed linear network that exchanges two
120	banks of values, with prescribed signs, and restores every auxiliary
121	value. A wire's fixed place in the network is called its role. To use
122	the network on an array, regard a row as the complete ordered suffix,
123	including all active address fields, at a fixed prefix and row index.
124	Distribute rows cyclically among the $W$ roles, padding the row count
125	for each prefix to a multiple of $W$. Let $V$ now denote the node volume
126	after padding. All role streams have the same local address set and each
127	contains $V/W$ bits. A scalar gate is then applied
128	pointwise to matching addresses on the roles that it touches.
129	
130	The representation of a role's array may change along the network.
131	At a source, gate, or sink $v$, choose an invertible linear operator
132	$D_v$ on the space of arrays indexed by the common address set. We call $D_v$ its frame: the stored
133	array is $D_vg$ when the logical array is $g$. All incidences of one
134	gate have the same frame. Along an edge from $u$ to $v$, the operator
135	$D_vD_u^{-1}$ changes the stored array from $D_ug$ to $D_vg$.
136	At a pointwise linear gate $G$, the common frame commutes with the gate:
137	\[
138	 G(D_vg_1,\ldots,D_vg_t)=D_vG(g_1,\ldots,g_t).
139	\]
140	The supplied input needs no preliminary change of frame: its logical
141	interpretation is defined by applying the inverse input frame. Thus the
142	intermediate frames cancel, and a route from input role $w$ to output
143	role $\rho(w)$ applies
144	$D_{\mathrm{sink}(\rho(w))}D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}^{-1}$, together with
145	its prescribed scalar sign. Undoing the role exchange and those signs
146	leaves the endpoint operator on every role array, including the roles
147	that carried auxiliary scalar values.
148	
149	For the bit procedure, that endpoint operator is an address shear:
150	two fields, written as vectors $H,D$ over a common residue ring, are
151	updated by $(H,D)\mapsto(H+D,D)$. Two further linear-cost address
152	updates complete their interchange. For the numerical procedure, the
153	endpoint operator becomes the simultaneous $H_0$ layer after diagonal
154	phase operations and a dyadic scale. The intermediate frames are chosen
155	so that every edge can be implemented by smaller calls to the same
156	procedure.
157	
158	The finite construction in Section~\ref{sec:finite-networks} attaches
159	subspaces of a fixed $m$-dimensional space to its gates and terminals.
160	The subspaces at adjacent vertices are nested. Their dimension changes
161	count the smaller operations needed on an edge, with an additional
162	source contribution in the bit construction. The construction uses
163	three-element subsets: gather and scatter create coefficients depending
164	on intersection size, and auxiliary wires cancel the unwanted
165	coefficients. Orthogonality of the corresponding indicator vectors permits
166	the subspace assignments. The decisive property is that the total
167	number $s$ of smaller calls satisfies $s<Wm$.
168	
169	A recursive call at parameter $mf$ therefore uses $s$ calls at parameter
170	$f$, each on a stream of volume $V/W$. The parameter counts field
171	digits for address interchange and selected axes for a numerical layer.
172	After dividing cost by volume, multiplying the parameter by $m$
173	increases the recursive contribution by $s/W<m$. This strict inequality
174	is the source of the power saving. The later tape and arithmetic
175	estimates preserve it, including the work of changing numerical address
176	coordinates. Those changes are implemented by whole-chunk moves and
177	controlled shifts, followed by a deterministic correction of the
178	explicitly identified exceptional addresses.

180	\subsection{From transforms to the exact product}
181	
182	The remaining proof places these procedures inside the multiplication
183	reduction and accounts for every change of representation.
184	First, the radix-digit coefficient list is placed on a product of
185	distinct prime cyclic axes by a Chinese-remainder map that preserves
186	convolution. Section~\ref{sec:assembly} implements this map through
187	triangular controlled shifts and charged axis moves. Gaussian
188	resampling then expresses each source Fourier transform through a
189	power-of-two tensor transform. Section~\ref{sec:resampling} retains the
190	source and target coordinate permutations in the transform identity,
191	so they need not be executed as separate full sorts.
192	
193	Next, Bluestein's chirp identity converts the middle transform,
194	including its target permutation, into normalized cyclic convolution.
195	A phase twist changes the last cyclic coordinate into a polynomial
196	modulo $y^r+1$; its negative wrap gives precisely the original cyclic
197	wrap after the twist is removed. Sections~\ref{sec:synthetic-layouts}
198	and~\ref{sec:exact-ring-products} compute convolution on the remaining
199	axes over this polynomial ring. The two forward synthetic transforms
200	retain the same frequency order through their pointwise product, and
201	the opposite transform consumes that order. Their polynomial products
202	use signed packing and the established $O(n\log n)$ multiplier as an
203	ordinary subroutine.
204	
205	Finally, the source permutation retained during resampling cancels
206	across the two forward source transforms, their pointwise product,
207	and the opposite-sign transform. Section~\ref{sec:assembly} removes
208	the known normalizations and digit scales, proves that the recovered
209	coefficient error is strictly below $1/2$, and propagates carries to
210	obtain the exact binary product. A compatible choice of rational
211	parameters makes all terms in its cost table fit Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.

269	\subsection{Historical context and inherited methods}
270	
271	Karatsuba's recursive construction, published jointly
272	with Ofman in 1962, gave a binary multiplication circuit of size
273	$O(n^{\log_2 3})$~\cite{KaratsubaOfman1962}. Toom's subsequent use of polynomial
274	evaluation and interpolation gave circuit size
275	$n\exp(O(\sqrt{\log n}))$, and hence $O(n^{1+\eta})$ for every fixed
276	$\eta>0$~\cite{Toom1963}. These early results were formulated in terms of
277	automata and logical networks. Cook adapted Toom's method to the
278	Turing-machine setting; the contemporary account of Sch\"onhage and
279	Strassen credits this adaptation explicitly
280	\cite[Section~1, p.~282]{SchonhageStrassen1971}.
281	
282	In the multitape Turing model,
283	Sch\"onhage and Strassen proved the bound
284	$O(n\log n\log\log n)$ in 1971~\cite{SchonhageStrassen1971}.
285	F\"urer improved it to $n\log n\,2^{O(\log^* n)}$ in 2007, with a full
286	journal account in 2009~\cite{Furer2007,Furer2009}; here $\log^* n$ counts
287	iterated logarithms until a constant threshold is reached.
288	De, Kurur, Saha and Saptharishi developed a modular-arithmetic route to
289	the same scale~\cite{DeKururSahaSaptharishi2013}.
290	Later improvements made the exponential factor $8^{\log^* n}$ and then
291	$4^{\log^* n}$~\cite{HarveyHoevenLecerf2016,HarveyHoeven2019Lattice}.
292	Harvey and van der Hoeven proved the unconditional
293	$O(n\log n)$ bound~\cite{HarveyHoeven2021}.
294	
295	The multitape bounds just cited concern that fixed model. Sch\"onhage obtained
296	linear-time multiplication on storage-modification machines~\cite{Schonhage1980}.
297	Groff later gave a smaller-than-$\log n$ factor in a unit-cost RAM model
298	with constant-time arbitrary memory access, after polynomial preprocessing
299	whose cost is excluded from that bound~\cite[Sections~2 and~4]{Groff2019}.
300	Neither result establishes the bound in the fixed finite-tape model of
301	Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
302	
303	The transform methods behind these bounds also underlie the present
304	construction. Sch\"onhage--Strassen multiplication uses roots of unity in
305	Fermat-type residue rings, where certain multiplications become shifts.
306	F\"urer combines cheap polynomial roots of unity with more general roots,
307	reducing the frequency of expensive multiplications. Harvey and van der
308	Hoeven use Gaussian resampling to pass to multidimensional transforms with
309	power-of-two dimensions, then evaluate them using polynomial transforms
310	developed by Nussbaumer and Quandalle and subsequently by
311	Nussbaumer~\cite{NussbaumerQuandalle1978,Nussbaumer1980,HarveyHoeven2021}.
312	The Gaussian-gridding work of Dutt and Rokhlin is an earlier conceptual
313	precursor~\cite{DuttRokhlin1993}; Harvey and van der Hoeven discuss the
314	connection in~\cite[Section~4.4.3]{HarveyHoeven2021}. The quantitative
315	resampling and bit-cost estimates used here are those of the latter paper.
316	
317	More specifically, the proof adapts Harvey and van der Hoeven's
318	Gaussian-resampling identity, contraction bounds, and short-convolution
319	procedures~\cite[Theorem~4.2, Proposition~4.7 and Lemmas~4.8--4.12]{HarveyHoeven2021}.
320	Their framework already permits arbitrary dimension. Here the source and
321	target permutations remain in the transform identity, while the faster tape
322	procedures perform the required axis movements. Bluestein's conversion to
323	convolution~\cite{Bluestein1970} and the synthetic-root convolution algorithm
324	are retained; the latter follows the polynomial-transform construction
325	in~\cite[Section~2.4 and Section~3]{HarveyHoeven2021}. Signed coefficient
326	packing is a form of Kronecker substitution, with the fixed-tape version
327	of~\cite[Lemma~2.5]{HarveyHoeven2021} as a direct antecedent.
328	Calls to the established $O(n\log n)$ multiplier are ordinary subroutine
329	calls; they do not invoke the improved theorem recursively.
330	
331	\subsection{The finite-network ingredients}
332	
333	The subset-intersection construction in Section~\ref{sec:finite-networks}
334	has an earlier source outside multiplication. Alon's presentation of the
335	Frankl--Wilson construction~\cite{FranklWilson1981} gives low-degree
336	representations of complementary intersection graphs over different fields
337	\cite[Section~3, remark after the proof of Theorem~1.1]{Alon1998}.
338	At the prime $p=2$, its subsets have size three and the two polynomial evaluations
339	are the intersection count modulo two and the intersection count minus one.
340	These are the two pairing formulas used here. We change the ground-set
341	size and express the second pairing through a rational bilinear form.
342	
343	The gather and scatter operations, together with the side wires, have the
344	form of linear index-code decoding: a low-rank linear summary gives the
345	wanted coordinate plus contributions from known neighboring coordinates,
346	and those contributions are subtracted. Bar-Yossef, Birk, Jayram and Kol
347	establish the fitting-matrix formulation and this decoder
348	\cite[Section~3, proof of Theorem~5]{BarYossefBirkJayramKol2006}.
349	Lubetzky and Stav treat decoding over other fields and use related
350	intersection representations to separate their possible ranks
351	\cite[Proposition~2.1 and Section~2.3]{LubetzkyStav2009}.
352	These comparisons explain the algebraic role of the two fields here;
353	they do not supply the subspace labels on the subsequent network.
354	
355	Restoring scratch registers with arbitrary initial contents also has a
356	precise precedent. The transparent-computation construction of Buhrman,
357	Cleve, Kouck\'y, Loff and Speelman subtracts an initial register value,
358	performs a computation, adds the resulting value, and reverses the
359	computation~\cite[Section~3]{BuhrmanCleveKouckyLoffSpeelman2014}.
360	Our scratch schedule is the linear-readout version of that construction.
361	The rank reduction used for address shears is a singular-matrix Bruhat
362	factorization: after reversing the coordinate order, Grigor'ev's
363	upper-triangular factors become the two lower-triangular factors needed
364	here~\cite[Appendix~A.2, Proposition~14(c)]{Grigoriev1982}.
365	
366	The finite networks and their labels are proved directly in
367	Section~\ref{sec:finite-networks}. The additional requirements are the
368	three-stage bank exchange, nested subspaces with a strict total rank or
369	dimension deficit, and endpoint frames acting on every role. The tape
370	implementations then turn that deficit into the volume-normalized
371	recurrences of Sections~\ref{sec:tape-interchange}
372	and~\ref{sec:fast-butterfly-layers}, including the costs of addressing,
373	padding, coefficient growth, and finite precision. The cited decoding,
374	restoration, and factorization results provide ingredients; these further
375	properties are established in the present proof.
376	
377	\subsection{Lower-bound scope and matrix transposition}
378	
379	Sch\"onhage and Strassen conjectured $n\log n$ as the optimal order of
380	multiplication cost~\cite[Section~1]{SchonhageStrassen1971}. In the present
381	fixed-tape model, an eventual lower bound for every multiplication machine means that, for
382	each fixed machine $A$, there are constants $c_A>0$ and $N_A$ such that
383	$T_A(n)\ge c_A n\lg n$ whenever $n\ge N_A$.
384	Its negation requires one machine satisfying
385	$\liminf_{n\to\infty}T_A(n)/(n\lg n)=0$.
386	The power saving proved here gives a limit of zero through all input lengths,
387	which is a stronger conclusion.
388	
389	Harvey and van der Hoeven consider a binary transposition machine
390	supplied an integer $m\ge1$ and a $k\times k$ binary matrix, where
391	$k=\lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor$. They proved that if every fixed such machine
392	has worst-case cost $\Omega(m\lg m)$ through all sufficiently large
393	supplied values of $m$, then every fixed multiplication machine has the
394	corresponding eventual lower bound~\cite[Theorem~1.2]{HarveyHoeven2025}.
395	Combining their quantitative reduction~\cite[Corollary~6.2]{HarveyHoeven2025}
396	with Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives a deterministic fixed-tape algorithm
397	that transposes a row-major $k\times k$ binary matrix in
398	$O(k^2(\lg k)^{1-\kappa})$ time, with $\kappa$ as in
399	Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Section~\ref{sec:transposition} proves the more
400	general rectangular-matrix bound.
401	
402	This comparison concerns unrestricted computation on a fixed number of
403	one-dimensional tapes. Our address procedure forms XOR combinations of
404	intermediate data, even though its final effect is a permutation.
405	It therefore lies outside models restricted to moving data without such
406	computations; see~\cite[Section~1.4]{HarveyHoeven2025} for the distinction.

408	\subsection{Companion application to exact Fourier transforms}
409	
410	The complex phase network of Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface}
411	is also used in the companion manuscript~\cite[Section~1.1, Theorem~1.1
412	and Corollary~1.2]{OpenAIExactDFT2026}. That manuscript gives a single
413	algorithm for the exact discrete Fourier transform at every positive
414	transform length $n$. As $n\to\infty$, its cost is
415	$O(n(\log n)^{1-10^{-13}})=o(n\log n)$.
416	
417	The cost is measured in an exact complex-register model that assigns unit
418	cost to exact complex field operations. The algorithm accepts every
419	$x\in\mathbb C^n$, with no bound on its entries or on intermediate complex
420	magnitudes. Its computation on the input uses only addition, subtraction,
421	and multiplication by prepared input-independent scalars. The magnitudes
422	of those scalar coefficients are unrestricted as well.
423	
424	Integer operations and random access on $O(\log(n+2))$-bit words have unit
425	cost, with a fixed number of words for each address or integer. The model
426	supplies one specified Fourier root $\zeta_{D_*}$ of explicitly computable
427	order $D_*<1024n^3$. Scalar preparation, schedule construction, and index
428	work are charged. This is a separate application of the finite network,
429	with its own uniform array implementation. It is neither a bit-complexity
430	consequence nor a stable floating-point FFT consequence of the fixed-tape
431	multiplication theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.

433	\label{sec:streams}
434	
435	A machine has one fixed finite alphabet and one fixed finite number of
436	one-dimensional tapes. A step reads and writes at most one cell on each

442	combinations of intermediate data streams. The present section supplies
443	the elementary scans it uses. Every scan includes its counters and the

4047	leftward when the digits are formed.

4049	\subsubsection{The padded box and working precision}
4050	
4051	After obtaining $n$, compute the size parameters below with the
4052	separate setup costs stated in this subsection.  For sufficiently
4053	large $n$, put
4054	\[
4055	 b=\lceil\log_2n\rceil,\quad p=6b,\quad d=\lfloor b^\epsilon\rfloor,
4056	 \quad K=\lfloor d^c\rfloor.
4057	\]
4058	Take the power of two $T$ in $[4n/b,8n/b)$, and let
4059	$r=2^{\lceil(\log_2T)/d\rceil}$ and $\ell=\log_2r$.  Choose
4060	$d\ell-\log_2T$ of the $d$ axis lengths to be $r/2$ and the others to
4061	be $r$.  This gives
4062	\[
4063	 t_i\in\{r/2,r\},\qquad \prod_i t_i=T,\qquad t_d=r.
4064	\]
4065	Indeed $d\ell-\log_2T$ is an integer in $[0,d)$, so at least one axis
4066	has length $r$; choose it as the last axis.
4067	These definitions give
4068	\begin{equation}\label{eq:sizes}
4069	 Tp=\Theta(n),\quad d=\Theta(p^\epsilon),\quad
4070	 K=\Theta(p^{\epsilon c}),\quad
4071	 \ell=\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon}),\quad r=2^{\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon})}.
4072	\end{equation}
4073	The comparison constants can be fixed for every input length at once.
4074	For sufficiently large $b$, the bounds on $n,T$ give
4075	$b/2\leq\log_2T\leq b$. Since $p=6b$, $d=\lfloor b^\epsilon\rfloor$
4076	and $d\leq b$, they imply
4077	\[
4078	 \frac1{12}p^\epsilon\leq d\leq p^\epsilon,
4079	 \qquad \frac{p}{12d}\leq\ell\leq\frac{p}{3d}.
4080	\]
4081	Thus we fix $a_d=a_r=1/12$, $b_d=1$, $b_r=1/3$, and $C_\ell=1$
4082	in the layer and transform interfaces. Their pointwise bounds cover every
4083	computed pair $(d,r)$, including all choices arising at the same $p$.
4084	These bounds also give that $r$ exceeds every fixed power of $p$,
4085	$K/\log p\to\infty$, and
4086	$\ell/K\to\infty$.  There are eventually enough axes for the
4087	$O(\log d)$ reserved row axes and enough bits for all work blocks.
4088	
4089	Set
4090	\[
4091	 \alpha=\left\lceil(12d^2b)^{1/4}\right\rceil,
4092	 \qquad \gamma=2d\alpha^2,\qquad \eta=\frac1{4d}.
4093	\]
4094	The ceiling does not affect the needed bounds: for $A\ge1$,
4095	$\lceil A\rceil\le2A$, and hence
4096	\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma}
4097	 \alpha\le2(12d^2b)^{1/4},\qquad
4098	 \gamma<28d^2\sqrt b\le28b^{1/2+2\epsilon}\le28b^{2/3}.
4099	\end{equation}
4100	It follows that $2\le\alpha<\sqrt p$ eventually and $\gamma=o(b)$.
4101	For example $b\ge2^{24}$ implies $\gamma\le b/4$.

4103	\subsubsection{Prime source lengths}
4104	
4105	The distinct prime lengths $s_i$ must be close to the powers of two
4106	$t_i$: their product must occupy a fixed fraction of the padded box,
4107	while each ratio $t_i/s_i$ must leave enough separation for resampling.
4108	We verify both requirements for the parameters just chosen.
4109	
4110	The prime-interval result
4111	\cite[Lemma~5.1]{HarveyHoeven2021}, based on explicit estimates of
4112	Rosser and Schoenfeld~\cite{RosserSchoenfeld1962}, gives the following
4113	bound: for
4114	$0<\eta<1/4$ and $x>e^{2/\eta}$, the interval
4115	\[
4116	 (1-2\eta)x<q\leq(1-\eta)x
4117	\]
4118	contains at least $\eta x/(2\log x)$ primes. Here $\log$ is the natural
4119	logarithm. The size bounds in \eqref{eq:sizes} give
4120	$d=\Theta(p^\epsilon)$ and $\log r=\Theta(p/d)$.
4121	For large $n$ we have $d\geq2$, so
4122	$0<\eta<1/4$, and
4123	\[
4124	 \frac{\log(r/2)}d=\Theta(p^{1-2\epsilon})\longrightarrow\infty.
4125	\]
4126	Thus both $x=r/2$ and $x=r$ satisfy $\log x>8d=2/\eta$.
4127	For either choice, the stated lower bound for the number of primes is
4128	$x/(8d\log x)$ and exceeds $d$:
4129	indeed, $\log x=\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon})$, whereas
4130	$\log(8d^2\log x)=O(\log p)=o(\log x)$, so $x>8d^2\log x$ eventually.
4131	The two intervals are disjoint because
4132	$(1-\eta)r/2<(1-2\eta)r$ for $\eta<1/4$, and both intervals lie above
4133	$2$. We may therefore choose distinct odd primes satisfying
4134	\[
4135	 (1-2\eta)t_i<s_i\leq(1-\eta)t_i.
4136	\]
4137	Every $\gcd(s_i,t_i)$ equals one because $t_i$ is a power of two.
4138	Put $S=\prod_i s_i$. Multiplying the lower bounds on $s_i$ and
4139	applying strict Bernoulli inequality gives
4140	\[
4141	 \frac ST>
4142	 \left(1-\frac1{2d}\right)^d>\frac12
4143	 \qquad(d\geq2).
4144	\]
4145	Together with $s_i<t_i$, this gives $T/2<S<T$.
4146	Writing $\theta_i=t_i/s_i-1$, the upper bound on $s_i$ gives
4147	$\theta_i\geq\eta/(1-\eta)>\eta$. Therefore
4148	\[
4149	 \alpha^4\theta_i>\frac{12d^2b}{4d}=3db\geq6b=p.
4150	\]
4151	The choice of $\alpha$ gives
4152	$\alpha=\Theta(p^{1/4+\epsilon/2})$, and \eqref{eq:gamma} already
4153	ensures $2\leq\alpha<\sqrt p$ for large $n$. We also have
4154	$t_i\leq r\leq T<8n/b<2^{6b}=2^p$.
4155	Thus every hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:no-sort-resampling} holds for
4156	all sufficiently large input lengths. The superpolynomial growth of $r$
4157	established above also supplies the setup condition in
4158	Lemma~\ref{lem:tensor-resampling}.
4159	
4160	The machine finds these primes by scanning the two intervals
4161	deterministically and testing each candidate by trial division through
4162	its square root. Testing every candidate would visit $O(r)$ candidates
4163	and at most $O(\sqrt r)$ trial divisors per candidate. Elementary
4164	division on $O(\log r)$-bit integers and management of a list of at most
4165	$d$ selected primes give the conservative bound
4166	$O(dr^{3/2}\operatorname{poly}(p))$. Its logarithm is
4167	\[
4168	 O(\log p+\log r)=O(\log p+p/d)=o(p).
4169	\]
4170	Since $p=6\lceil\log_2 n\rceil=\Theta(\log n)$, the search takes
4171	$n^{o(1)}=o(n)$ time.
4172	All remaining scalar setup, including comparisons for fixed rational
4173	powers, modular inverses,
4174	prime products and shape descriptors, has cost polynomial in $p$.
4175	For example, $d=\lfloor b^{2^{-75}}\rfloor$ is found by binary search
4176	using exact comparisons $d^{2^{75}}\le b$; the exponent is fixed.
4177	The same procedure computes $K$ and all other fixed rational powers.
4178	All primes and length parameters are therefore generated by the machine;
4179	they are not advice.

4181	\subsubsection{The radix-digit polynomials}
4182	
4183	Write the two inputs as polynomials in $2^b$, each with
4184	$q=\lceil n/b\rceil$ nonnegative digits.  Their product has degree at most
4185	\[
4186	 2q-2<2n/b\le T/2<S.
4187	\]
4188	Thus convolution modulo $x^S-1$ has no nonzero wraparound.  Every product
4189	coefficient obeys
4190	\begin{equation}\label{eq:capacity}
4191	 0\le c_j\le q(2^b-1)^2<2^{3b},
4192	\end{equation}

4195	\subsection{An explicit cyclic-convolution layout}
4196	
4197	To use the source tensor, we first place the ordinary coefficient stream
4198	in its tensor order. Agarwal and Cooley used the Chinese remainder
4199	theorem to convert one cyclic convolution into multidimensional cyclic
4200	convolution~\cite{AgarwalCooley1977}. The following map uses that
4201	algebraic split, with coordinate powers that make the change of order a
4202	sequence of controlled cyclic shifts.
4203	
4204	Let $s_1,\ldots,s_d$ be the pairwise coprime
4205	source lengths, let $S=\prod_i s_i$, and put
4206	\[
4207	 P_i=\prod_{j<i}s_j,\qquad \mu_i=P_i^{-1}\pmod{s_i}.
4208	\]
4209	Here $P_i$ denotes an integer prefix product, not a Fourier-coordinate
4210	permutation.  The assignment
4211	\[
4212	 \Phi:\mathbb C[x]/(x^S-1)\longrightarrow
4213	 \mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/(x_1^{s_1}-1,\ldots,x_d^{s_d}-1),
4214	 \qquad x\longmapsto\prod_i x_i^{\mu_i}
4215	\]
4216	respects $x^S=1$, so it defines an algebra map.  The target monomial
4217	group has size $S$, and the image of $x$ has order $S$, because each
4218	$\mu_i$ is a unit and the $s_i$ are pairwise coprime.  Its powers
4219	therefore run through all target basis monomials exactly once.  Hence
4220	$\Phi$ is an isomorphism and preserves cyclic convolution.
4221	
4222	Every ordinary coefficient index has a unique mixed-radix expression
4223	\[
4224	 k=\sum_{j=1}^d a_jP_j,\qquad 0\le a_j<s_j.
4225	\]
4226	The coordinate of $\Phi(x^k)$ in axis $i$ is
4227	\begin{equation}\label{eq:triangular-crt}
4228	 b_i=a_i+\mu_i\sum_{j<i}a_jP_j\pmod{s_i}.
4229	\end{equation}
4230	Indeed terms with $j>i$ are divisible by $s_i$, and $\mu_iP_i=1$ modulo
4231	$s_i$.  Numerical order of $k$ is lexicographic order of
4232	$(a_d,\ldots,a_1)$.  Insert the padding in one nested scan of the full
4233	box $\prod_i[0,t_i)$ in this lexicographic order, with $a_d$ the
4234	outermost counter and $a_1$ the innermost.  At an address satisfying
4235	$a_i<s_i$ for every $i$, copy the next original coefficient record;
4236	at every other address, write a zero record.  The valid addresses
4237	occur in the original coefficient order, so each record is copied to
4238	its intended mixed-radix address.  To delete the padding after the
4239	inverse axis reorder, use the same enumeration, copying the record at
4240	each valid address and skipping the record at each invalid address.
4241	
4242	Store the nested binary counters consecutively on a fixed work tape.
4243	Their total width is $\sum_i\log_2t_i=\log_2T=O(p)$, and the stored
4244	bounds $s_i$ also have total width $O(p)$.  At each of the $T$
4245	addresses, updating the counters, testing validity, and handling the
4246	$O(p)$-bit record therefore cost $O(p)$ steps, including counter-head
4247	returns.  Each insertion or deletion scan costs $O(Tp)$.
4248	
4249	Now reorder the complete padded axes to $(a_1,\ldots,a_d)$.  In this
4250	physical order, the coordinates with
4251	indices below $i$ precede coordinate $i$.  Update the targets in the
4252	order $i=d,d-1,\ldots,1$ using \eqref{eq:triangular-crt}.  When target
4253	$i$ is updated, none of its lower-index controls has yet changed, so
4254	the offset is computed from the original digits $a_j$ required by the
4255	formula.
4256	
4257	To specify the action on padded addresses, let
4258	\[
4259	 \mathcal P=\prod_i[0,t_i),\qquad \mathcal V=\prod_i[0,s_i)
4260	\]
4261	be sets of integer addresses.  On a fixed control prefix, rotate the
4262	valid target interval $[0,s_i)$ by the offset in
4263	\eqref{eq:triangular-crt} and fix $[s_i,t_i)$.  If any lower-index
4264	control is invalid, use the identity.  This defines a bijection of
4265	$\mathcal P$: for fixed controls and spectators it is a cyclic
4266	permutation of the valid target interval and the identity elsewhere.
4267	Each step preserves $\mathcal V$ and its complement.  Consequently
4268	zero padding remains zero after every step.  An inverse is explicit:
4269	process $i=1,\ldots,d$, subtracting the same expression formed from the
4270	already recovered lower coordinates; then undo the axis reorder and
4271	perform the deletion scan just described.
4272	
4273	Each triangular update is a prefix-controlled cyclic shift.  The
4274	controls precede its target in the current physical order.  For each
4275	prefix, prepare the offset, split the valid target interval into its
4276	two consecutive pieces, and merge those pieces in the opposite order.
4277	Every target position carries its full spectator suffix as a block;
4278	the invalid interval is copied unchanged.  There are at most $T/t_i$
4279	control prefixes for target $i$.  For any fixed setup degree $C$, all
4280	offsets therefore cost $O(dTp^C/r)=o(Tp)$ to prepare, since
4281	$t_i\ge r/2$ and $r$ exceeds every fixed power of $p$.
4282	
4283	The axis widths are $\ell$ or $\ell-1$.  To exchange two adjacent axes
4284	of unequal width, move the longer axis's leading bit outside their
4285	equal-width pair, swap that pair by the proved chunk-swap procedure,
4286	and put the leading bit at its new position.  This adds a fixed number
4287	of linear passes to the equal-width swap cost.  Reversing all axes
4288	uses $O(d^2)$ such moves.  Therefore the map $\Phi$, its inverse, and
4289	their padding operations cost
4290	\[
4291	 O\bigl(Tp\,d^2(1+\ell^\tau)\bigr).
4292	\]
4293	This construction describes payload movement from address $a$ to its
4294	new address.  It is distinct from the operator convention
4295	$(R_cz)_j=z_{cj}$ used for Fourier dilations, which moves a payload
4296	from address $j$ to $c^{-1}j$.

4298	\subsection{Complex convolution by a coefficient twist}
4299	
4300	The power-of-two complex convolution used in the chirp identity is
4301	obtained from the synthetic convolution by a coefficient twist.
4302	Put $\mathcal R=\mathcal R_r=\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$ and
4303	$\zeta=e^{\pi i/r}$.  The map
4304	\[
4305	 \Theta:\mathbb C[x_d]/(x_d^r-1)\longrightarrow\mathcal R,
4306	 \qquad x_d\longmapsto\zeta y
4307	\]
4308	is well defined, since $(\zeta y)^r=(-1)(-1)=1$.  On the bases
4309	$(x_d^k)_{0\le k<r}$ and $(y^k)_{0\le k<r}$ it is diagonal,
4310	multiplying coefficient $k$ by the nonzero number $\zeta^k$.  It is therefore an
4311	isomorphism, with inverse multiplying that coefficient by
4312	$\zeta^{-k}$.  Both exact maps preserve the coefficient sup norm.
4313	For an explicit check on the wrap, write $k+l=j+hr$, where
4314	$h\in\{0,1\}$.  A product term after twisting and negacyclic reduction

4315	has factor
4316	\[
4317	 \zeta^{k+l}(-1)^h=\zeta^j(\zeta^r)^h(-1)^h=\zeta^j.
4318	\]
4319	Untwisting therefore recovers the cyclic coefficient with the correct
4320	sign.  We next specify how this linewise map meets the ring-convolution
4321	interface.  Put $M=\prod_{i<d}t_i=T/r$.  For a complex array $f$ on
4322	$\prod_{i=1}^d\mathbb Z/t_i\mathbb Z$, with $t_d=r$, define
4323	\[
4324	 (\iota f)_{\boldsymbol j}
4325	   =\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}f_{\boldsymbol j,k}y^k,
4326	 \qquad
4327	 \boldsymbol j\in\prod_{i<d}\mathbb Z/t_i\mathbb Z.
4328	\]
4329	This identifies the scalar tensor with an array of $M$ records in
4330	$\mathcal R$. As maps of values, $\iota$ and $\iota^{-1}$ preserve norms
4331	and grids. Write
4332	$(D_\pm f)_{\boldsymbol j,k}=\zeta^{\pm k}f_{\boldsymbol j,k}$.
4333	The linewise extension of $\Theta$ is $\iota D_+$, with inverse
4334	$D_-\iota^{-1}$.  Consequently, with $\mathcal M_r$ from
4335	Section~\ref{sec:exact-ring-products}, normalized complex cyclic
4336	convolution is
4337	\[
4338	 \mathcal M_{\mathbb C}(f,g)
4339	   :=D_-\iota^{-1}
4340	       \mathcal M_r(\iota D_+f,\iota D_+g)
4341	    =\frac{f*g}{T}.
4342	\]
4343	Here $\mathcal M_r$ convolves the first $d-1$ axes over $\mathcal R$,
4344	whereas $*$ on the right convolves all $d$ scalar axes.  The division
4345	by $T$ is already part of $\mathcal M_r$.  The maps $D_\pm$ and
4346	$\iota^{\pm1}$ are isometries, so $\mathcal M_{\mathbb C}$ is also a
4347	bilinear contraction.

4349	\subsubsection{Computed complex convolution}
4350	
4351	For the tape representation, use the scalar format of
4352	Section~\ref{sec:resampling}, with $w_{\rm c}=p+2$ bits per component.
4353	For $p\geq2$, this satisfies $p+2\leq w_{\rm c}\leq2p$, so fix $C_w=2$
4354	and instantiate the synthetic component width as $w=w_{\rm c}$.

4356	imaginary words in the same coefficient order: the last coordinate is

4358	$\iota^{-1}$ change only the shape descriptor and require no payload
4359	movement when these component formats agree.

4361	For the synthetic transform calls, the machine writes the header
4362	\[
4363	 \mathcal T=\Gamma(p)\Gamma(d)\Gamma(r)\Gamma(K)\Gamma(w_{\rm c})
4364	       \prod_{i=1}^{d-1}\Gamma(t_i).

4454	\subsubsection{The source transform}
4455	
4456	For a source disk-grid tensor of norm at most $.5$, write
4457	$\widetilde{\mathscr F}$ for the following procedure: apply the linewise
4458	approximation to $\mathcal A$, apply the
4459	computed chirp transform $\widetilde{\mathscr C}$, apply the linewise
4460	approximation to $\mathcal B_0$, and multiply the grid numerators
4461	exactly by $2^\gamma$.  Its exact counterpart is
4462	\[
4463	 \mathscr F=2^\gamma\mathcal B_0QF_{\boldsymbol t}\mathcal A
4464	            =RF_{\boldsymbol s}.
4465	\]
4466	Here an exact counterpart replaces every numerical subroutine by the
4467	exact map it approximates and omits truncations.  The source arrays are
4468	stored in the padded power-of-two box, with zeros outside the valid
4469	source coordinates.

4471	$\gamma$ zero bits to each word gives the exact scaled numerator in the
4472	known signed width $w_{\rm c}+\gamma$. For the stated input norm, the

4475	$2^p$, so a scan removes only leading sign-extension bits and returns
4476	the same integers in $w_{\rm c}$ bits. This scan costs
4477	$O(T(w_{\rm c}+\gamma))=O(Tp)$ and leaves the padded zero records zero.

4479	\[
4480	 \widetilde{\mathscr F}^{+}(z)
4481	   =\overline{\widetilde{\mathscr F}(\overline z)};
4482	\]

4484	Lemma~\ref{lem:chirp-permutation}.

4486	\subsection{The multiplication algorithm}
4487	
4488	The source-transform procedures now supply the three transforms needed
4489	for the radix-digit convolution. Read each stored operand backward from
4490	its least significant end in groups of $b$ bits. This produces the radix-$2^b$ digits
4491	$a_0,\ldots,a_{q-1}$ in increasing coefficient order.  Buffer each
4492	group on a fixed work tape and read it back most significant bit first,
4493	reversing its least-significant-first input order; pad the final short
4494	group with leading zeroes.
4495	For digit $a_j$, write the exact grid numerator
4496	$a_j2^{p-b-2}$ in a signed $w_{\rm c}$-bit real word, followed by a zero
4497	$w_{\rm c}$-bit imaginary word. This exponent is nonnegative
4498	because $p=6b$, and the represented value is exactly $a_j2^{-b-2}$.
4499	Append $S-q$ zero coefficient records.  Buffering and ordering the
4500	groups costs $O(n)$, including the one partial group's padding, and
4501	writing the $S$ records costs $O(Sp)$.
4502	Together with the initial count and copies, this input conversion
4503	costs $O(n+Sp)=O(Tp)$; all $n$ input bits, including leading zeroes,
4504	are retained before the final group is padded.
4505	
4506	With these streams prepared, perform the following operations.
4507	\begin{enumerate}
4508	\item Apply the coefficient-address map $\Phi$, with its padded layout, to obtain
4509	source arrays $u,v$.  Their coefficients are exact $p$-bit grid
4510	values of norm less than $1/4$.
4511	\item Compute $\widetilde{\mathscr F}(u)$ and
4512	$\widetilde{\mathscr F}(v)$.
4513	\item Multiply corresponding complex coefficients exactly and truncate
4514	each real and imaginary part toward zero to $p$ fractional bits, writing
4515	the result in the common $w_{\rm c}$-bit component format.
4516	Denote the resulting source array by $z$.
4517	\item Compute $\widetilde{\mathscr F}^{+}(z)$ and multiply its grid
4518	numerators exactly by $S$, retaining the denominator $2^p$ and writing
4519	each component in signed width $w_{\rm c}+b$. Denote the represented
4520	dyadic array by $\widetilde w$.
4521	\item Multiply the grid numerators of $\widetilde w$ exactly by
4522	$2^{2b+4}S$, again retaining the denominator $2^p$, and write each
4523	component in signed width $w_{\rm c}+4b+4$. Round the represented real
4524	values to the nearest integers. At each valid address, write the rounded
4525	coefficient in one signed $(3b+1)$-bit word, most significant bit first;
4526	at every padded address,
4527	write a zero word of that width. Supply this local payload width to
4528	$\Phi^{-1}$ and apply it, including removal of the address padding, to
4529	restore the ordinary coefficient order.
4530	\item Propagate radix-$2^b$ carries in increasing coefficient order.
4531	Write the resulting bits from least to most significant on a work tape,
4532	then reverse that stream and output exactly $2n$ bits in
4533	most-significant-first order.
4534	\end{enumerate}

4536	The two occurrences of $S$ in this algorithm undo different
4537	normalizations.  By \eqref{eq:source-permutation-cancel}, the exact
4538	counterpart after the three transforms is $(u*v)/S^2$, so after the
4539	first scale it is $w=(u*v)/S$.  The second scale gives
4540	$2^{2b+4}(u*v)$, whose inverse image under $\Phi$ is the original
4541	integer coefficient convolution.  The next subsection verifies the
4542	disk bounds needed by every call and proves that the final error is
4543	less than $1/2$; it also justifies the rounding, carries, and output
4544	length.

4913	\paragraph{Setup and exceptional streams across all calls.}
4914	We next separate setup at recursion nodes from work repeated for every
4915	polynomial record or every Gaussian line.  Here a visit means a node
4916	of the layer or address-layout recursions, or one of their round and
4917	group invocations.  The internal recursion of the established integer
4918	multiplier and the iterations of the quoted Gaussian algorithms are
4919	already included in their separately charged running times.
4920	The layer and address-layout recursions have constant branching and
4921	depth $O(\log p)$, and the number of their rounds and base-$m$ groups
4922	is polynomial in $p$.  Choose a fixed exponent $A$ so that their
4923	total number of visits is at most $p^A$, and a fixed $C$ bounding
4924	descriptor setup performed once per visit by $p^C$ steps.  This setup then
4925	costs at most $p^{A+C}=o(Tp)$.

4927	At a layer or synthetic-transform visit that processes polynomial
4928	records, there are at most $O(T/r)$ such records, including the
4929	bounded row padding.  Every relevant child keeps the whole
4930	length-$r$ polynomial suffix.  Consequently $O(p^C)$ descriptor or
4931	address work per record, over these visits, costs at most
4932	$O(Tp^{A+C}/r)=o(Tp)$.  Setup before each Gaussian line call has a

432	  \section{The machine model and elementary streams}
433	\label{sec:streams}
434	
435	A machine has one fixed finite alphabet and one fixed finite number of
436	one-dimensional tapes. A step reads and writes at most one cell on each
437	tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Fixed tracks and finitely
438	many work tapes change time by a fixed factor. We distinguish moving one
439	digit in a fixed radix, which needs a bounded number of scans, from
440	interchanging fields whose numbers of digits grow. The latter permutation
441	will be realized in Section~\ref{sec:tape-interchange} by computing XOR
442	combinations of intermediate data streams. The present section supplies
443	the elementary scans it uses. Every scan includes its counters and the
444	return of its tape heads.
445	
446	\subsection{Array order and elementary scans}
447	
448	For a positive integer $a$ write $[a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}$.
449	An array with address set $[a_1]\times\cdots\times[a_t]$ is stored in
450	lexicographic order, with the first coordinate most significant.  Its
451	entries are bits unless a record width is specified.  A trailing record
452	of $B$ bits can equivalently be regarded as a final address field $[B]$.
453	An address is implicit in an entry's position in this ordered stream; it
454	is not stored beside every data bit.
455	The \emph{logical volume} $V$ is the number of stored data bits.  Work
456	tapes and duplicate streams are charged in time but do not increase $V$
457	in recurrences.  All the fields discussed below are nonempty.  A call
458	with an empty array is handled directly.
459	
460	An address permutation $f$ moves the entry at $x$ to $f(x)$.  Thus its
461	action on an array $A$ is $(fA)(f(x))=A(x)$.  Adjacent fields which are
462	irrelevant to an operation may be replaced by a single field whose length
463	is their product.  In particular, the elementary procedures below have a
464	fixed number of formal address fields even when a surrounding algorithm
465	has a growing list of coordinates.  Lengths and positions are supplied in
466	canonical binary on descriptor tapes; no additional tape head is attached to an
467	address coordinate. Each elementary call receives a fixed number of
468	collapsed canonical lengths. Constructing them from a longer surrounding
469	list is work of the caller; recursive calls below construct their own
470	collapsed descriptors within their stated bounds.
471	
472	When one address field is designated as a row field, collapse the fields
473	before it to a prefix $[P]$ and those after it to a suffix $[B]$.  If the
474	row field has range $[R]$, a \emph{row} at prefix $p$ and row index $r$
475	is the complete consecutive block $\{p\}\times\{r\}\times[B]$.
476	Every row therefore contains $B$ bits in the same suffix order.
477	
478	For headers that concatenate a list of positive integer parameters, we use
479	the self-delimiting code
480	\begin{equation}
481	 b_v=\lfloor\log_2v\rfloor+1,\qquad
482	 \Gamma(v)=0^{b_v-1}\operatorname{bin}_{b_v}(v),\qquad
483	 |\Gamma(v)|=2b_v-1\quad(v\ge1).
484	 \label{eq:integer-descriptor-code}
485	\end{equation}
486	The initial zeroes specify how many further bits follow the first one,
487	so concatenated codes can be read in order. We use this code when an
488	interface specifies a header; elementary calls still receive the fixed
489	number of canonical binary lengths described above.
490	
491	\begin{lemma}[Elementary stream operations]
492	\label{lem:elementary-streams}
493	Fix a radix $q\ge2$.  Each of the following operations on an array of
494	volume $V$ takes $O(V)$ steps on a fixed number of one-dimensional tapes:
495	\begin{enumerate}
496	\item any fixed permutation of the pair of digit values at two specified
497	radix-$q$ positions, whether or not the positions are adjacent;
498	\item moving one specified radix-$q$ digit to another position, preserving
499	the order of the intervening positions;
500	\item splitting on a specified radix-$q$ digit, applying a fixed
501	pointwise map to aligned streams, and merging them back;
502	\item for positive integers $P,R,B$, within each prefix of an array on
503	$[P]\times[R]\times[B]$, splitting
504	whole rows cyclically into a fixed number $W$ of streams, and, when $W$
505	divides $R$, merging those streams in any fixed order of the row classes.
506	\end{enumerate}
507	The bounds include shape preparation, counter initialization and resets,
508	and returning or clearing the visited portions of work tapes.  Their
509	constants may depend on the fixed radix, the fixed pointwise map, and the
510	fixed number of row classes.
511	\end{lemma}
512	
513	\begin{proof}
514	For the first operation split into $q^2$ streams according to the two
515	specified digits.  With these digits fixed, the order of all remaining
516	digits is unchanged by the permutation.  Enumerate output addresses in
517	their required order and read the stream prescribed by the two preimage
518	digits.  For a digit move use $q$ streams instead.  The same observation
519	shows that splitting on one digit gives streams with the same remaining
520	address set in the same order.  Scan their aligned entries, apply the
521	fixed pointwise map, and merge according to the output digit; this proves
522	the third operation.  For the fourth, write $r=Wg+w$, where
523	$0\le w<W$, and send the whole row to stream $w$.  If $W$ divides $R$,
524	each stream has address set $[P]\times[R/W]\times[B]$, indexed by the
525	prefix, $g$, and the unchanged suffix.  Thus the streams have the same
526	shape and each has volume $V/W$.  The inverse merge, with any fixed
527	permutation of the classes, reads them in the specified cyclic order.
528	
529	Here are the counter details used in these scans and later ones.  A
530	binary counter is stored with its head at the least significant end.
531	For a counter of width $w$, incrementing or decrementing and returning
532	this head over $L$ consecutive counts costs $O(L+w)$: the number of
533	visits to position $j$ is $O(1+L/2^j)$. The width term is paid when
534	initializing the counter and is absorbed by its complete range scan.  A countdown of
535	length $L$ can be initialized, reset, and tested for underflow in
536	$O(\log(2L))=O(L)$ time.  Keep a local copy of its length on a dedicated
537	track, so a reset does not search a larger descriptor.  For a nested scan
538	of a fixed number of nonempty ranges, the reset of a range is charged to
539	the scan of that range.  Induction on the number of ranges therefore gives
540	linear total counting cost.  A fixed number of empty pieces in a split
541	can be charged to the adjacent nonempty combined range.
542	
543	Only a fixed number of collapsed lengths are needed.  Computing these
544	lengths and the initial counter values by ordinary binary arithmetic
545	takes $O((\log(2V))^C)$ steps for a fixed $C$.  This is $O(V)$ uniformly
546	in $V\ge1$, after increasing a fixed constant.  Each stream is scanned a
547	fixed number of times, and every rewind, copy, or erasure is over a
548	region whose length was charged to that scan.  Delimiters and the fixed
549	number of tracks require only a fixed alphabet enlargement.
550	\end{proof}
551	
552	The next operations are linear because their target field follows their
553	control fields.  This order will be preserved whenever they are invoked.
554	
555	\begin{lemma}[Controlled shifts and fixed rational scalings]
556	\label{lem:ordered-affine-streams}
557	Fix a prime $q$, a fixed number of control fields, and finitely many
558	rational coefficients whose denominators are prime to $q$.  Whenever a
559	coefficient is used as a unit, also require its numerator to be prime to
560	$q$.  Put $Q=q^b$, $b\ge1$.
561	Suppose a target field $y\in[Q]$ follows its control fields, each control
562	used in an offset having $O(b)$ digits.  An update
563	\[
564	 y\longmapsto y+a(\text{controls})\pmod Q
565	\]
566	costs $O(V)$ if the offset can be prepared in $b^{O(1)}$ time from the
567	fixed number of control values.  In particular, this holds for a fixed
568	rational linear combination of them, specialized modulo $Q$.
569	Multiplication of $y$ by any of the specified rational units, and its
570	inverse, also costs $O(V)$.  Arbitrarily long intervening spectator
571	fields and suffix records are permitted.
572	\end{lemma}
573	
574	\begin{proof}
575	Fix all fields before the target, and let the suffix length be $B$ bits.
576	The resulting fiber consists of $Q$ consecutive blocks of length $B$.
577	For an offset $a\in[Q]$, split these blocks at $Q-a$.  Append the two
578	pieces to two tapes, doing so successively for all prefix fibers.  In the
579	merge read the second piece and then the first piece for each prefix.
580	The pieces have become the two consecutive ranges $[0,a)$ and $[a,Q)$
581	of the new target coordinate.  Recompute $a$ when starting that prefix in
582	the merge.  Initializing these two piece lengths and returning the heads
583	of the relevant control counters is included in the $b^{O(1)}$ offset
584	work.  Since
585	\[
586	 b^C=O(q^b)=O(Q)
587	\]
588	for each fixed $C$, this work is absorbed by the $QB\ge Q$ bits of the
589	fiber.  Unrelated spectator counters are incremented by ripple counting;
590	their entire contents are not consulted when computing the offset.
591	
592	For positive fixed integer $c$ prime to $q$, the permutation
593	$y\mapsto cy\pmod Q$ has $c$ increasing pieces, classified by
594	\[
595	 j=\left\lfloor\frac{cy}{Q}\right\rfloor,
596	 \qquad 0\le j<c.
597	\]
598	Prepare their endpoints once for this $Q$, split each fiber into these
599	$c$ streams, and enumerate the output coordinate $y'=0,\ldots,Q-1$.
600	The required stream is the unique $j\in[c]$ for which
601	$y'+jQ\equiv0\pmod c$.  Uniqueness follows from $\gcd(Q,c)=1$;
602	the corresponding $y=(y'+jQ)/c$ lies in $[Q]$.  The stream choice is
603	maintained by a finite residue counter.  Reversing the roles of this
604	split and merge implements multiplication by $c^{-1}$ modulo $Q$.
605	
606	Negation leaves the block at zero fixed and reverses the order of the
607	other $Q-1$ blocks.  Push these blocks consecutively to a temporary tape.
608	Popping gives their order reversed, but also reverses the bits in each
609	block.  Reverse each popped block on a second temporary tape before
610	writing it, restoring its internal order.  Every bit is moved a bounded
611	number of times.  The same procedure is repeated for successive fibers;
612	the temporary stack is emptied and its head returned locally.  A signed
613	rational unit is a composition of these integer multiplications, inverse
614	multiplications, and possibly negation.  Its description is fixed.
615	
616	The nested scan and reset analysis of
617	Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-streams} applies to all these operations.  In
618	particular, copying a suffix-length counter at every target position
619	costs $O(\log(2B))\le O(B)$ at that position.  It does not introduce a
620	factor $\log V$ per bit.
621	\end{proof}
622	
623	When coefficients have a denominator $d$ prime to $q$, their reductions
624	modulo $q^b$ can be computed by the extended Euclidean algorithm using
625	ordinary tape arithmetic.  The dimension and all original coefficients
626	are fixed, so these preparations have polynomial cost in $b$.  Nothing
627	in Lemma~\ref{lem:ordered-affine-streams} assumes unit-cost arithmetic.
628	
629	For later use, fixed-width signed fixed-point binary addition,
630	subtraction, sign change, and multiplication or division by a fixed
631	power of two are streaming operations of linear bit cost, provided
632	enough integer and fractional guard bits have been allocated for exact
633	results. If an input record is most-significant-bit first, reverse it onto
634	the arithmetic work tape. With least significant bits first on that tape,
635	propagate carries using finite control. Reverse the completed record if
636	its required external order is opposite.
637	This convention separates the order of bits inside a record from the
638	lexicographic order of records. Each required reversal is a linear pass
639	and is charged.

1394: \begin{lemma}[The cost of a rational matrix shear]
1395: \label{lem:matrix-shear}

1397: matrices.  There is a fixed odd prime $q$ such that the following holds.

1475: \begin{proposition}[Power-width interchange with rows]

1975: \label{lem:packed-selected-bit-rectangle}

1978: $(\chi_1,\chi_2,\chi_3)$ be a permutation of $(x,y,z)$.

1982:  \times[N_2]\times[2^L]_{\chi_3}\times[N_3].

1985: $N_0,\ldots,N_3,R,K,f,\rho$ as a fixed number of canonical binary
1986: integers, together with the finite permutation of the chunk names, as
1987: in Section~\ref{sec:streams}. Put
1988: \[

1559	\paragraph{A fixed-tape depth-first schedule.}
1560	Here we complete the implementation assertion used in
1561	\eqref{eq:swap-recurrence}.  Reserve $W$ role tapes, a fixed set of
1562	I/O and elementary-operation work tapes, one parking stack tape, and a
1563	separate descriptor stack.  Although $W$ is large, it is fixed.
1564	At a call boundary all reusable work tapes, other than the current I/O
1565	and local descriptor, are empty and their heads are at their origins.
1566	The parking and descriptor heads are at the tops of their stacks.
1567	
1568	Before a recursive call, append the $W-1$ inactive role streams to the
1569	parking stack in a fixed order, with separators.  Copy the active stream
1570	to the child I/O area, and erase the parent role tapes while traversing
1571	their current contents.  Push the parent descriptor and its finite
1572	program counter to the descriptor stack.  The role and work tapes are
1573	now available to the child, using the same tapes at every depth.
1574	On return, copy the child output into the designated active role.
1575	Pop the inactive streams in reverse order.  To recover a stream in its
1576	original direction, prepare its destination to the known length and
1577	write the popped symbols from the destination's right end toward its
1578	left end.  Erase the popped stack cells as they are left.  This uses
1579	linear time and ends with the parking head at the previously saved top.
1580	No scan passes through a parked ancestor.  Cleanup is always limited to
1581	the region visited by the current call; a reused tape is not swept to
1582	the largest position ever visited by an ancestor.

1584	Each push, pop, copy, positioning operation, or erasure moves $O(V)$
1585	symbols at a parent node.  There are only the fixed number $s$ of child
1586	calls.  This gives precisely the additional $O(V)$ term claimed above,
1587	even though each child itself has volume $V/W$.  Temporary storage is
1588	therefore not substituted for logical volume in the factor $s/W$.

1591	payload is one bit.  Let $V_0$ be the volume at the root of one

1593	of any depth-$j$ child.  Here $j\le k_0=\log_m e_0$.  The root row
1594	count is at least $W^{k_0}$, so at depth $j$ it is still at least one.
1595	Both original chunk ranges remain present: digits outside the current
1596	subchunks become spectators rather than being removed.  Hence
1597	\[
1598	 V_j\ge q^{2e_0},\qquad

\section{Fast simultaneous synthetic butterfly layers}
\label{sec:fast-butterfly-layers}

We now apply the complex network to a common butterfly layer on several
axes. The array has complete address set
\[
 [P]\times[2^K]^D\times[S],\qquad 1\le D\le d,
\]
with $P,S\ge1$, in lexicographic order. Its $D$ consecutive $K$-bit
chunks each select the bit at one common offset $0\le\rho<K$, counted
from the least significant
end. Each address carries a polynomial record with $r$ complex
coefficients, initially in the unit disk on the grid
$2^{-p}\mathbb Z[i]$, with $\Theta(p)$ bits per real or imaginary
component. The intended operation is the tensor product
of $H_0(u,v)=((u+v)/2,(u-v)/2)$ on the $D$ selected bits, acting
coefficientwise and preserving all other address fields.

The parameters will satisfy
\[
 d=\Theta(p^\epsilon),\qquad K=\lfloor d^c\rfloor,
 \qquad r=2^{\Theta(p/d)},\qquad c>0,\quad 0<\epsilon<1.
\]
The exponents and comparison constants are fixed, and we impose their
further restrictions in Proposition~\ref{prop:simultaneous-layer}.
Two consequences explain the layout. The polynomial length $r$ grows
faster than every fixed power of $p$, so a scan of a record pays for
polynomial work on its address. Also $K/\log p\to\infty$, which will
make the exceptional set in a packed change of address bits small enough
to repair by sorting. We will obtain cost $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$, with
$\lambda'<1$ and $V$ the logical bit volume, whereas separate butterfly
factors would require $D$ whole-array passes.

We first construct tensor products of the auxiliary two-point kernel
$C$ from Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface}. Its phase
frames express a $C$ tensor product using smaller groups of
selected bits, separated by binary changes of basis. We implement those
changes by moving whole address chunks. Splitting complete rows among
the network's wire roles then reduces the volume of each recursive
call. Finally, we bound the intermediate dyadic values and convert the
completed $C$ layer to the normalized $H_0$ layer. The entire layer is
evaluated exactly before one final truncation.

\subsection{Phase frames for a simultaneous butterfly layer}
 \section{Synthetic transforms and their tape layout}
\label{sec:synthetic-layouts}

We now implement the normalized Fourier transforms needed for
convolution.  Their entries will be short polynomials in a quotient
where the required roots of unity act by exact signed permutations
of coefficient lists.  We also specify where each frequency entry
is stored, because the opposite transform consumes that same order
after a pointwise product.

The polynomial roots and radix-two butterflies belong to the fast
polynomial-transform method of Nussbaumer and
Quandalle~\cite{NussbaumerQuandalle1978,Nussbaumer1980}; we use the
form developed in~\cite[Section~2.4 and Lemma~3.2]{HarveyHoeven2021}.
The work here is to apply the simultaneous layers on a suitable tape
layout and retain the resulting frequency order through convolution.

For an integer $r\geq 2$ that is a power of two, put
\[
 \mathcal R_r=\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1),\qquad
 \left\|\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}z_k y^k\right\|_\infty
       =\max_{0\leq k<r}|z_k|.
\]
We always use representatives of degree less than $r$.  Multiplication
by $y^a$, for any integer $a$, permutes the coefficients and changes
some signs; consequently it is an isometry for this norm.  For arrays
over $\mathcal R_r$, the same notation denotes the maximum over all
coefficients in all entries.  A disk array has norm at most one.  A
$p$-bit grid array has real and imaginary coefficient parts in
$2^{-p}\mathbb Z$.  For any array, let $Q_p$ truncate each real and
imaginary coefficient part toward zero to this grid.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \|Q_p z-z\|_\infty<\sqrt2\,2^{-p},\qquad
 \|Q_p z\|_\infty\leq\|z\|_\infty.
 \label{eq:transform-truncate}
\end{equation}

\subsection{Roots, butterflies, and stored frequency order}

For a power of two $t$ dividing $2r$, define $\omega_t=y^{2r/t}$.
For $z\in\mathcal R_r^t$ and $0\leq j<t$, set
\[
 (F_t^-z)_j=\frac1t\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\omega_t^{-jk}z_k,
 \qquad
 (F_t^+z)_j=\frac1t\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\omega_t^{jk}z_k.
\]
Every power of $\omega_t$ is an isometry, and each transform entry is
an average of $t$ such images.  Thus both transforms are contractions.
The ring has zero divisors, so we verify character cancellation
directly instead of dividing by $\omega_t^j-1$.

\section{Resampling with the permutations left in the transform}
\label{sec:resampling}

The transform lengths needed for the integer product are pairwise coprime,
whereas the synthetic transforms use powers of two. Gaussian resampling
connects these two shapes. Its usual implementation sorts twice on each
coordinate. We retain both permutations in the transform formula and
compute that formula directly. This section proves the resulting interface,
including its tape cost when the number of coordinates grows.

For an integer $q\geq 1$, write
\[
 (F_q u)_k=\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}u_j e^{-2\pi i jk/q},
 \qquad
 (F_q^+ u)_k=\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}u_j e^{2\pi i jk/q}.
\]
All subscripts on a vector of length $q$ are taken modulo $q$.
The vector norm is the maximum modulus of its coordinates. All operator
norms are induced by this norm: $\|L\|=\sup_{\|u\|\leq1}\|Lu\|$.
Each normalized Fourier transform above is a contraction, since each
output averages inputs multiplied by complex numbers of modulus one. Coordinate
permutations preserve the norm.
For an integer precision $p\geq1$, put
\[
 \mathbb D_p=\{2^{-p}(a+ib):a,b\in\mathbb Z,\ a^2+b^2\leq 2^{2p}\}.
\]
For storage between completed scalar routines, put $w_{\rm c}=p+2$.
Represent $2^{-p}(a+ib)\in\mathbb D_p$ by a signed $w_{\rm c}$-bit
two's-complement word for $a$, followed by one for $b$, with each word
written most significant bit first. A coordinate list is the
concatenation of these fixed-length records in its stated order. Since
$|a|,|b|\leq2^p<2^{w_{\rm c}-1}$, this format includes both signs of
every permitted numerator, including $-2^p$ and $2^p$.
An approximation $\widetilde L:\mathbb D_p^a\to\mathbb D_p^b$
to a linear contraction $L:\mathbb C^a\to\mathbb C^b$ has error $E$
if $2^p\|\widetilde L u-Lu\|<E$ for every input in $\mathbb D_p^a$.
The approximation itself need not be linear. Composing such algorithms
adds their errors: at each step, insert the exact map at the computed
input and use its contraction bound on the accumulated input error.

We use the established $O(N\log N)$ integer multiplier of
Harvey and van der Hoeven~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{HarveyHoeven2021}
for the shorter integer records that occur below. We also use their
Lemma~2.12: for integer precision $p>100$ and integers $k>1$, $0\leq j<k$,
one can compute $\widetilde\zeta\in\mathbb D_p$ with
$2^p|\widetilde\zeta-e^{2\pi i j/k}|<2$ in time
$O(\max(p,\log k)^{1+\delta})$, for every fixed $0<\delta<1/8$.
Throughout this section, numbered citations to that paper refer to its
author-hosted 45-page manuscript.

\subsection{The normalized convolution interface}

For arrays on $\prod_i\mathbb Z/t_i\mathbb Z$ with values in
$\mathcal R_r$, let $*$ denote cyclic convolution in the displayed
axes and define
\[
       \mathcal M_r(f,g)=\frac{f*g}{rM}=\frac{f*g}{T}.
\]
For a fixed output coefficient, each of the $M$ first cyclic
addresses determines one second address, and each of the $r$ first
polynomial indices determines one second index modulo $r$.  The
negacyclic wrap supplies the sign.  Thus that coefficient averages
$rM$ signed scalar products, and $\mathcal M_r$ is a bilinear
contraction:
\[
 \|\mathcal M_r(f,g)\|_\infty
       \leq\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_\infty.
\]
If the other operand is a disk array, replacing one operand changes
the output by at most the norm distance between its two values.
